---
title: "Watching Forest Change with Esri Wayback and Sentinel-2"
output: bookdown::html_document2
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  dpi = 150
)
```

```{r load, include = FALSE}
# Data from data-raw/wayback_change.R; the article itself makes no network call.
library(terra)
d <- function(f) file.path("wayback-change", f)

meta <- utils::read.csv(d("meta.csv"))
cap <- utils::read.csv(d("captures.csv"))
pk <- utils::read.csv(d("picks.csv"))
s2s <- utils::read.csv(d("s2.csv"))

cap$capture_date <- as.Date(cap$capture_date)
pk$date <- as.Date(pk$date)
pk$capture_date <- as.Date(pk$capture_date)
sub <- cap[cap$sub_metre, ]
win <- unlist(meta[c("win_xmin", "win_xmax", "win_ymin", "win_ymax")])
win_km <- (win[["win_xmax"]] - win[["win_xmin"]]) / 1000
# ground size of a tile pixel at the box's latitude
zoom_m <- function(z) round(156543.03392 / 2^z * cos(meta$box_lat * pi / 180), 2)
own <- pk[match(sub$capture_date, pk$capture_date), ]

fmt <- function(x) format(as.Date(x), "%Y-%m-%d")
wb <- lapply(fmt(sub$capture_date), function(x) rast(d(paste0("wb_", x, "_window.tif"))))
s2_years <- s2s$year
s2 <- lapply(s2_years, function(y) rast(d(paste0("s2_", y, ".tif"))))

fpc <- utils::read.csv(d("floodplain.csv"))
fp <- vect(fpc$wkt, crs = "EPSG:32609")
# the outline colour comes from the gq registry's floodplain style, so no hex
# literal appears in this article; the white beneath it is a halo over imagery
fp_col <- gq::gq_reg_main()$layers$floodplains$fill$color
draw_fp <- function(lwd = 1.5) {
  lines(fp, col = "white", lwd = lwd + 1.5)
  lines(fp, col = fp_col, lwd = lwd)
}

# Picks for the key years that have no capture of their own
key <- pk[!format(pk$date, "%Y") %in% format(sub$capture_date, "%Y"), ]
key_days <- function(y) {
  r <- key[format(key$date, "%Y") == y, ]
  paste0(fmt(r$capture_date), ", ", abs(r$days_from_date), " days ",
         if (r$days_from_date < 0) "before" else "after", " ", y, "-07-01")
}

panel_label <- function(lab) {
  u <- par("usr")
  text(u[1] + 0.03 * (u[2] - u[1]), u[4] - 0.06 * (u[4] - u[3]), lab,
       adj = c(0, 1), font = 2, col = "white", cex = 0.9)
}
```

Esri Wayback keeps the past versions of the World Imagery basemap, so the
sub-metre satellite images of a place can be looked at in the order they were
taken. drift reads them with `dft_wayback_releases()`, `dft_wayback_captures()`,
`dft_wayback_pick()` and `dft_wayback_fetch()`. Wayback images are sharp enough to
show single trees, but a place is often imaged only every few years. Where that leaves
gaps, `dft_stac_composite()` adds a 10 m Sentinel-2 image for every summer.

This article follows one `r meta$box_km2` km² box of forest and river valley in
northern British Columbia, the area of the New Graph post
[Sentinel-2 Ortho Mosaics with STAC and gdalcubes](https://www.newgraphenvironment.com/new_graphiti/posts/2026-01-08-stac-ortho-mosaics/).
Looking through those mosaics by hand puts the main changes to forest cover in
2018, 2020, 2022 and 2023. The maps outline the published floodplain of the
Bulkley River watershed group (`co_ff04`, the functional floodplain on the
coho-accessible stream network), which covers `r fpc$area_ha` ha of the box.

## What changed between 2014 and 2020?

```{r fig-window, fig.height = 2.38, fig.cap = paste0("One ", win_km, " km square of the box in the three sub-metre Wayback images, taken ", paste(fmt(sub$capture_date), collapse = ", "), ", read from tiles of ", paste(zoom_m(own$zoom), collapse = ", "), " m and drawn on one 0.5 m grid. Forest covers the centre in the first two; by the third a clearing with a spur road has opened there, and a bare track runs along the edge of the valley floor at the bottom. The blue line is the edge of the floodplain. The scale bar is 200 m.")}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2), bg = "white")
for (i in seq_along(wb)) {
  plotRGB(wb[[i]], scale = 255, mar = NA, axes = FALSE)
  draw_fp(1.2)
  panel_label(fmt(sub$capture_date[i]))
  if (i == 1) sbar(200, "bottomleft", type = "bar", divs = 2, below = "", label = "",
                   col = "white", lwd = 1)
}
par(op)
```

In the first two images the centre of the square is forest. By the third, a
clearing with a spur road has opened there, between two arms of the floodplain
and outside both, and a bare track runs along the edge of the valley floor at
the bottom. Between the second and third images there are four years, and
Wayback holds nothing in between to say when the cutting happened. The
Sentinel-2 composites below narrow that down.

## When was a Wayback image taken?

A Wayback **release** is the World Imagery basemap as Esri published it on one
date. Each release is a mosaic of **captures**, single satellite images taken
on their own dates, often years apart. So a release date says only that its
captures are older than that date. To look at a place in a given year, choose
the capture, not the release.

Over this box, the `r meta$releases_searched` releases from
`r fmt(meta$release_from)` to `r fmt(meta$release_to)` draw from just
`r nrow(cap)` dated captures, and `r nrow(sub)` of them are sub-metre. The
`r fmt(sub$capture_date[1])` capture was still in the release of
`r fmt(sub$release_last[1])`. All `r sub$n_releases[nrow(sub)]` releases from
`r fmt(sub$release_first[nrow(sub)])` on show the
`r fmt(sub$capture_date[nrow(sub)])` capture, so the newest release, of
`r fmt(meta$release_to)`, shows the ground as it was in
`r format(sub$capture_date[nrow(sub)], "%Y")`.

## Which captures image this area?

`dft_wayback_captures()` reads each release's metadata and returns the
captures it draws over the area. Over a polygon a release can draw more than
one capture, so each row also carries `cover`, the share of the polygon where
that capture is the one on top.

```{r captures-code, eval = FALSE}
library(drift)

bbox <- c(xmin = -126.17545, ymin = 54.36161, xmax = -126.12615, ymax = 54.38908)
aoi <- sf::st_bbox(bbox, crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_transform(32609) |>   # the box's UTM rectangle, so rasters are full rectangles
  sf::st_bbox() |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_as_sf()

rel <- dft_wayback_releases()
rel <- rel[rel$release_date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"), ]
cap <- dft_wayback_captures(aoi, zoom = 16:18, releases = rel)
```

Reading the metadata of every release is network time, up to a quarter of an
hour here. After that it is cached, and a rerun takes under a minute.

```{r captures-table}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Taken = fmt(cap$capture_date),
    Source = cap$source,
    `Resolution (m)` = cap$res_m,
    `Largest cover` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cap$cover_max),
    Releases = cap$n_releases,
    `First release` = fmt(cap$release_first),
    `Last release` = fmt(cap$release_last),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = paste0("Every dated capture drawn over the box by the ",
                   meta$releases_searched, " releases searched. Largest cover is ",
                   "the largest share of the box the capture is drawn on in any one release.")
)
```

The `r fmt(sub$capture_date[2])` capture never covers more than
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sub$cover_max[2])` of the box. Its releases draw the
older capture on the rest.

## Which capture is nearest each year?

`dft_wayback_pick()` returns, for each target date, the capture taken nearest
to it, and the release and zoom to fetch it from. When several releases serve a
capture, the pick prefers the newest. Over a polygon that release may show the
capture on only part of the area: in the last release serving the
`r fmt(sub$capture_date[1])` capture, it covers
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sub$cover_last[1])` of the box. Keeping, for
each capture, only the releases where it covers the most of the box avoids
that.

```{r pick-code, eval = FALSE}
cap <- cap[cap$res_m < 1, ]
cap <- cap[cap$cover >= ave(cap$cover, cap$capture_date, FUN = max) - 0.001, ]
pick <- dft_wayback_pick(cap, as.Date(c("2014-07-01", "2016-07-01", "2018-07-01",
                                        "2020-07-01", "2022-07-01", "2023-07-01")))
```

```{r picks-table}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Target = fmt(pk$date),
    Capture = fmt(pk$capture_date),
    `Days from target` = pk$days_from_date,
    Release = pk$release_id,
    `Release date` = fmt(pk$release_date),
    Zoom = pk$zoom,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "The capture picked for each target date. Negative days are a capture before the target."
)
```

None of 2018, 2022 or 2023 has a capture of its own. 2018 gets
`r key_days("2018")`. 2022 gets `r key_days("2022")`, and 2023 gets
`r key_days("2023")`.

## How are the captures fetched so they line up?

`dft_wayback_fetch()` reads one release's tiles at one zoom and returns a
three-band raster, cached as a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. Giving every call the
same `crs` and `res` puts the captures on one grid, so they can be compared cell
for cell.

```{r fetch-code, eval = FALSE}
chips <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(pick)), function(i) {
  dft_wayback_fetch(aoi, pick$release_id[i], pick$zoom[i], crs = "EPSG:32609", res = 0.5)
})
```

A fetch over a polygon shows whatever its release draws there, so a panel
labelled with one capture shows that capture only where it is the one on top.
In each capture's release, that capture is the one drawn over the whole square
of the first figure.

```{r fig-overview, fig.width = 4.2, fig.height = 4.1, fig.cap = paste0("The whole box in the ", fmt(sub$capture_date[nrow(sub)]), " capture, at 5 m. The white square is the ", win_km, " km square of the first figure, and the blue line the edge of the floodplain. The scale bar is 1 km.")}
ov <- rast(d("wb_overview.tif"))
op <- par(mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2), bg = "white")
plotRGB(ov, scale = 255, mar = NA, axes = FALSE)
draw_fp()
rect(win[["win_xmin"]], win[["win_ymin"]], win[["win_xmax"]], win[["win_ymax"]],
     border = "white", lwd = 2)
sbar(1000, "bottomleft", type = "bar", divs = 2, below = "", label = "", col = "white")
par(op)
```

## What happened after 2020?

Sentinel-2 images the box every few days. `dft_stac_composite()` masks cloud
in each scene and takes the median of what is left over a window of months, so
it gives one image a year built from the clear days. A June–July composite shows the ground as it was in
those two months, so a change that first appears in one panel happened after
the start of the previous panel's window and before the end of this one's.

```{r composite-code, eval = FALSE}
s2 <- dft_stac_composite(aoi, years = c(2018, 2020, 2022, 2023), months = 6:7,
                         crs = "EPSG:32609")
```

```{r fig-s2, fig.height = 6.9, fig.cap = paste0("The box in Sentinel-2 June–July median composites at 10 m, ", paste(s2_years, collapse = ", "), ", with one brightness stretch shared by all four panels, so a difference in brightness is in the data and not in the display. The white square is the ", win_km, " km square of the first figure, and the blue line the edge of the floodplain. The scale bar is 1 km.")}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3), bg = "white")
for (i in seq_along(s2)) {
  plotRGB(s2[[i]], scale = 255, mar = NA, axes = FALSE)
  draw_fp(1.2)
  rect(win[["win_xmin"]], win[["win_ymin"]], win[["win_xmax"]], win[["win_ymax"]],
       border = "white", lwd = 1.5)
  panel_label(paste(s2_years[i], "Jun–Jul"))
  if (i == 1) sbar(1000, "bottomleft", type = "bar", divs = 2, below = "", label = "",
                   col = "white")
}
par(op)
```

The centre of the square is still forest in the 2018 composite and bare in 2020. So the
clearing that Wayback shows between `r fmt(sub$capture_date[2])` and
`r fmt(sub$capture_date[3])` was cut between June 2018 and July 2020. By 2022 it
is greening, and a new bare patch has opened just south-west of it. The 2023
composite shows the largest change of the four. Pale ground covers much of the
floodplain's valley floor across the south of the box, and new bare strips run
east from it through the forest. No release up to `r fmt(meta$release_to)` has a sub-metre capture of the 2022
or 2023 change.

## What are the limits?

- Over this box, sub-metre captures are years apart and the newest was taken on
  `r fmt(sub$capture_date[nrow(sub)])`, so Wayback shows nothing after it.
- A fetch over a polygon is a mosaic of whatever its release draws: the release
  picked for `r fmt(sub$capture_date[2])` shows that capture on
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sub$cover_max[2])` of the box and the
  `r fmt(sub$capture_date[1])` capture on the rest.
- The `r fmt(sub$capture_date[2])` capture has cloud and cloud shadow over the
  south-centre of the box.
- The three captures come from different sensors, in June and September, at
  different sun and view angles, so colour, shadow and leaf-out differ between
  them as well as the ground, and they are not co-registered to one another.
- The `r fmt(sub$capture_date[3])` capture is lower in contrast than the two before it.
- The first two captures are read from zoom `r own$zoom[1]` tiles
  (`r zoom_m(own$zoom[1])` m) and the third from zoom `r own$zoom[3]`
  (`r zoom_m(own$zoom[3])` m), the deepest zoom covering the whole box in each
  release, so part of the difference in sharpness is the zoom.
- Sentinel-2 at 10 m does not resolve single trees, and a composite dates a
  change only to the span from the start of one window to the end of the next.
- The 2023 composite is brighter across the whole box (median red reflectance
  `r s2s$red[s2s$year == 2023]`, against `r min(s2s$red[s2s$year != 2023])` to
  `r max(s2s$red[s2s$year != 2023])` in the other years), so not all of its pale
  ground is new.

The rasters and tables here come from
[`data-raw/wayback_change.R`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/drift/blob/main/data-raw/wayback_change.R).
